body.text: A tax year (taxation year) is the period that governs how Canadian corporations claim SR&ED incentives under the Income Tax Act. Bill C-15 reforms apply to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024; Form T661 is due 18 months after year-end; expenditure limits are prorated for short years; and unused ITCs carry back three years or forward 20.
Executive Summary and Statutory Architecture

Canada's research and development (R&D) fiscal incentive framework is anchored by the federal Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program, which represents the single largest federal source of financial support for industrial innovation, supporting more than 24,160 businesses annually. Statutorily codified within the federal Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)), the program operates through a dual-mechanism architecture that separates the deduction of qualifying R&D expenditures from the generation of investment tax credits (ITCs). Under Section 37 of the Income Tax Act, taxpayers carrying on business in Canada are permitted to pool and deduct 100% of qualified current—and, following recent legislative reforms, qualified capital—SR&ED expenditures in the taxation year incurred, or carry those undeducted expenditure pools forward indefinitely to offset future business income. Concurrently, Subsections 127(5), 127(9), 127(10.1), and Section 127.1 of the Income Tax Act establish a volume-based Investment Tax Credit regime that provides either a 35% enhanced refundable tax credit or a 15% basic tax credit on qualified SR&ED expenditures.

Between 2024 and 2026, the Canadian SR&ED landscape underwent its most consequential structural overhaul in more than a decade. Initiated via a two-phase Department of Finance public consultation launched on January 31, 2024, and reinforced by a $600 million four-year funding commitment in Budget 2024 (Fairness for Every Generation), the federal government sought to modernise the SR&ED program to improve scale-up retention, support hardware-intensive and compute-intensive innovation, and encourage domestic intellectual property (IP) ownership. While the December 2024 Fall Economic Statement initially proposed raising the enhanced expenditure limit to $4.5 million, Federal Budget 2025 expanded those parameters significantly. On March 26, 2026, Bill C-15, the Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1 (S.C. 2026, c. 3), received Royal Assent, enacting four foundational legislative pillars applicable to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, as well as depreciable property acquired after that date.

First, Bill C-15 doubled the enhanced expenditure limit under Subsection 127(10.2), raising the annual ceiling on qualified SR&ED expenditures eligible for the enhanced 35% ITC from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 and thereby increasing the maximum annual refundable federal cash benefit for qualifying corporations from $1,050,000 to $2,100,000. Second, the legislation widened the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada thresholds over which the $6,000,000 expenditure limit phases out, expanding the legacy $10,000,000 to $50,000,000 range to a substantially broader $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 band while adding an elective revenue-based alternative to the taxable capital phase-out. Third, reversing a decades-long statutory restriction that confined the 35% refundable credit exclusively to Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs), Bill C-15 enacted new definitions in Subsection 127(9) and phase-out rules in Subsections 127(10.6) and 127(10.62) allowing Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) resident in Canada to earn the 35% enhanced refundable ITC subject to a three-year average gross revenue test. Fourth, reversing the January 1, 2014 repeal of capital expenditure eligibility, Bill C-15 restored both Section 37 deductibility and Section 127 ITC eligibility for new or used depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, and capital lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, including the reinstatement of first-term and second-term Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) claims.

The second-order economic implication of the Bill C-15 reforms is a structural shift in the relative attractiveness of Canada for capital-intensive R&D—specifically artificial intelligence (AI) model training, graphics processing unit (GPU) cluster deployment, semiconductor design, clean technology pilot plants, and clinical-stage biotechnology. Between 2014 and 2024, Canada's exclusion of capital equipment forced domestic technology firms either to rely exclusively on operational cloud computing subscriptions (claimed as materials consumed or traditional overhead) or to absorb 100% of hardware acquisition costs outside the SR&ED credit base. By restoring capital expenditure eligibility alongside immediate 100% capital cost allowance (CCA) expensing for patents, data network infrastructure, and data processing equipment enacted for assets put into use before January 1, 2027, the Canadian tax system now provides immediate capital recovery for sovereign AI and deep-tech infrastructure. Furthermore, extending the 35% refundable credit to ECPCs removes the severe tax penalty that historically deterred research-intensive Canadian startups from listing on the Toronto Stock Exchange (TSX) or TSX Venture Exchange.

body.text: Federal SR&ED Tax Credit Mechanics, Rates, and Phase-Out Formulas
The Enhanced 35% Credit and Basic 15% Credit Structure

The federal SR&ED Investment Tax Credit operates on a two-tier volume-based rate structure under Section 127 of the Income Tax Act. Unlike jurisdictions that utilise incremental R&D tax credits at the federal level, Canada applies its federal credit percentages directly to the full volume of a taxpayer's net qualified SR&ED expenditures for the taxation year.

Under Subsection 127(10.1), a qualifying CCPC—as defined in Subsection 125(7) as a private corporation that is a Canadian corporation not controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons, by one or more public corporations (other than a prescribed venture capital corporation), or by any combination thereof—is entitled to an addition of 20 percentage points to the basic 15% ITC rate, yielding an enhanced ITC rate of 35% on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to its annual expenditure limit. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Subsection 127(10.1) as amended by Bill C-15 extends this identical 20-percentage-point addition (35% total rate) to an "eligible Canadian public corporation" (ECPC) as defined in Subsection 127(9).

Qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred by a CCPC or ECPC in excess of its annual expenditure limit, as well as all qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred by non-qualifying corporations (such as Canadian subsidiaries controlled by foreign multinational parents, large public corporations exceeding the ECPC revenue threshold, sole proprietorships, partnerships, and trusts), earn the basic ITC rate of 15% under Subsection 127(9).
Mathematical Formulation of the Expenditure Limit and Phase-Out Mechanics

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the base expenditure limit under Subsection 127(10.2) is $6,000,000, which represents a doubling of the $3,000,000 limit applicable to taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024. For a CCPC that does not file a revenue election under Subsection 127(10.31), the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is reduced linearly based on the taxable capital employed in Canada of the corporation—and all corporations associated with it under Subsection 256(1)—for the immediately preceding taxation year.

Under the amended Subsection 127(10.2) formula enacted by Bill C-15, the expenditure limit for a stand-alone CCPC with a full 365-day taxation year is expressed mathematically as: Expenditure Limit = $6,000,000 × [($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000]

where the variable A represents the excess of prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada over the $15,000,000 threshold, bounded between zero and $60,000,000: A = the lesser of $60,000,000 and (prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada − $15,000,000), with A nil where that taxable capital is $15,000,000 or less.

Consequently, if the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada of the CCPC and its associated group is $15,000,000 or less, A is nil and the corporation retains the full $6,000,000 expenditure limit. Once prior-year taxable capital exceeds $15,000,000, every $1,000,000 of additional taxable capital reduces the $6,000,000 expenditure limit by $100,000 (a linear reduction rate of 10%), until the expenditure limit reaches nil at $75,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital. The concept of taxable capital employed in Canada is determined under Part I.3 of the Income Tax Act (historically detailed in archived Interpretation Bulletin IT-532, Part I.3 – Tax on Large Corporations) and generally comprises share capital, retained earnings, surpluses, and debt obligations such as loans and advances, less an allowance for eligible investments in other corporations.

A critical technical nuance for tax auditors and corporate controllers is the divergence created by Bill C-15 between the SR&ED expenditure limit phase-out and the federal Small Business Deduction (SBD) phase-out under Section 125 of the Income Tax Act. While the SBD business limit of $500,000 continues to phase out over the $10,000,000 to $50,000,000 taxable capital range, the SR&ED expenditure limit now phases out over the $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 range (with the related qualifying income limit formula under the new rules also referencing $500,000 multiplied by [($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000], hitting zero at $75,000,000 of taxable capital for the 15% credit refundability test above the limit). Under the legacy regime for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the expenditure limit formula in Subsection 127(10.2) incorporated a grind where the qualifying income limit threshold was $40,000,000 rather than $60,000,000. Under the post-December 15, 2024 regime, growing associated groups must compute their Schedule 49 SR&ED expenditure limit allocation separately from their Small Business Deduction allocation.

body.text: Associated Corporations, Short Taxation Years, and the Revenue Election

Where a CCPC is associated with one or more other CCPCs in a taxation year within the meaning of Subsection 256(1), Subsection 127(10.21) mandates that the associated group share a single $6,000,000 expenditure limit reduced by the aggregate prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada of all associated CCPCs. The associated corporations must file an agreement in prescribed form—Schedule T2SCH49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit)—under Subsection 127(10.3) to allocate the group's expenditure limit among its members. If any member of the associated group fails to file the agreement within the statutory notice period after demand by the Minister of National Revenue, Subsection 127(10.4) empowers the Minister to allocate the expenditure limit among the corporations unilaterally. Furthermore, Subsections 127(10.22) and 127(10.23), operating alongside Subsections 127.1(2.2) and 127.1(2.3), provide targeted deemed non-association and anti-avoidance rules governing circumstances where corporations might otherwise be associated or where corporate structures are manipulated to multiply the refundable expenditure limit.

Under Subsection 127(10.5), two special proration rules govern irregular taxation years. First, if a corporation's taxation year is shorter than 51 weeks, its expenditure limit otherwise determined for the year must be prorated by the ratio of the number of days in the taxation year to 365. As illustrated in the CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, if Corporation P has a short taxation year running 184 days from July 1 to December 31, 2027, and is allocated a $3,000,000 share of an associated group's expenditure limit, its prorated expenditure limit under Subsection 127(10.5) is $1,512,328 ($3,000,000 × 184 ÷ 365). Second, specific rules under Subsection 127(10.5) apply when a CCPC has more than one taxation year ending in the same calendar year and is associated in two or more of those taxation years with another CCPC that has a taxation year ending in that same calendar year.

For Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)—defined in Subsection 127(9) as a taxable Canadian corporation resident in Canada whose shares are listed on a designated domestic or foreign stock exchange (such as the TSX, NYSE, or NASDAQ), that is not a CCPC, and that is not controlled, directly or indirectly, by one or more non-resident persons—the $6,000,000 expenditure limit under Subsection 127(10.6) is phased out based on the corporation's average annual gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years as reflected in its financial statements. Where an ECPC is a member of a consolidated corporate group that prepares "consolidated financial statements" within the meaning of Subsection 233.8(1) of the Income Tax Act (presenting the assets, liabilities, income, expenses, and cash flows of the group members as a single economic entity), Subsection 127(10.62) requires the $6,000,000 expenditure limit to be shared among all members of the consolidated group. In such cases, the three-year average annual gross revenue is computed using the consolidated financial statements of the group for the year in question, regardless of whether an individual entity joined or left the group during the year.

Crucially, under Subsection 127(10.31) (for a CCPC that is not associated with another corporation) and Subsection 127(10.32) (for the CCPC members of an associated group), a single CCPC or an associated group of CCPCs may formally elect, by filing a prescribed form, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, to forego the taxable capital phase-out formula in Subsection 127(10.2) and instead calculate its expenditure limit using the ECPC three-year average gross revenue phase-out method. For associated CCPCs making this election, the calculation requires aggregating the average annual revenue reflected in the financial statements of each corporation that is a member of the group for the taxation year in question over the preceding three fiscal years, irrespective of whether those corporations were associated throughout that entire three-year window. This election provides substantial relief to capital-intensive, pre-revenue or low-revenue CCPCs—such as clean energy developers, semiconductor fabricators, and late-stage clinical biotechnology companies—whose balance sheets carry more than $15,000,000 in debt and share capital (which would otherwise grind down their expenditure limit under the taxable capital test) but whose three-year average gross revenue remains low.
Refundability Matrix and Carryforward / Carryback Provisions

The cash-flow value of the SR&ED Investment Tax Credit is governed by Section 127.1 of the Income Tax Act, which differentiates refundability based on both the taxpayer's corporate status and whether the underlying qualified expenditures are of a current or capital nature. For qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs earning the enhanced 35% ITC on expenditures up to their expenditure limit, 100% of the unclaimed balance of the 35% ITC earned on qualified SR&ED current expenditures and the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) is fully refundable in cash. By contrast, for qualified SR&ED expenditures of a capital nature acquired after December 15, 2024, that earn the enhanced 35% ITC rate, Section 127.1 restricts cash refundability to 40% of the unclaimed balance of the 35% ITC earned in the year (yielding an immediate 14% cash refund on eligible capital expenditure, while the remaining 60% of the 35% credit—representing 21% of the capital cost—remains available to offset Part I tax payable or to be carried back or forward).

When a qualifying CCPC incurs qualified SR&ED expenditures in excess of its expenditure limit (or earns the basic 15% ITC while remaining within the qualifying income and taxable capital thresholds), 40% of the unclaimed balance of the basic 15% ITC earned in the year on both current and capital expenditures is refundable in cash (representing a 6% cash refund), with the remaining 60% of the credit available as a non-refundable offset against Part I tax. Conversely, for non-qualifying corporations—such as foreign-controlled Canadian subsidiaries and public corporations that do not qualify as ECPCs—the 15% basic ITC is completely non-refundable (0% refundability) and may only be applied under Subsection 127(5) to reduce federal Part I income tax otherwise payable.

Under Subsection 127.1(3), any SR&ED ITC that is refunded to a taxpayer under Section 127.1 in a taxation year is statutorily deemed to have been deducted under Subsection 127(5) to reduce Part I tax otherwise payable in that year. Consequently, refunded ITCs immediately reduce the taxpayer's unclaimed ITC pool available for carryback or carryforward. As illustrated in the CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, if a claimant earns $15,000 of ITC in Year 2 and utilizes or receives a refund of a portion, the claimant may carry back up to $3,000 to offset Part I tax in Year 1 and utilize the remaining $12,000 in Year 2 subject to applicable refundability rules. Any remaining unapplied and unrefunded SR&ED ITCs may be carried back up to 3 preceding taxation years or carried forward for up to 20 subsequent taxation years. Finally, under Subsection 127(9) and Section 37, any federal SR&ED ITC that is utilised (either applied to reduce Part I tax or refunded in cash) in a taxation year reduces the taxpayer's deductible Section 37 SR&ED expenditure pool in the following taxation year; where the pool is reduced below zero or current expenditures have already been deducted, the recaptured federal ITC amount is included directly in taxable business income in the following year.
Qualifying SR&ED Expenditures (QREs) and Cost Eligibility Rules
Direct Labour, Support Work, and Specified Employees

Salaries and wages consistently constitute the largest component of qualified SR&ED expenditures for Canadian claimants. To qualify under Section 37 and Subsection 127(9), salaries and wages must be incurred in respect of employees who are "directly engaged" in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. The CRA's administrative policy and Tax Court jurisprudence strictly establish that whether an employee is directly engaged in SR&ED depends entirely on the hands-on technical tasks performed by the individual, rather than the employee's corporate title or academic credentials. Eligible labour encompasses two distinct categories of work defined in Subsection 248(1). The first category is direct basic research, applied research, or experimental development, which includes hands-on scientific or engineering experimentation, hypothesis formulation, prototype design, coding of experimental algorithms, and analysis of test results. The second category is eligible support work, which covers work that is commensurate with the needs of, and directly in support of, basic research, applied research, or experimental development, restricted exclusively to the eight statutory disciplines enumerated in Subsection 248(1): engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, and psychological research.

Administrative, clerical, legal, human resources, routine quality control, market research, and commercial sales activities are statutorily excluded from SR&ED eligibility. Direct supervision of technical staff performing hands-on SR&ED qualifies as directly engaged labour only to the extent that the supervisor is providing technical direction on the experimental methodology rather than general corporate management. Furthermore, for "specified employees"—defined in Subsection 248(1) as an employee who does not deal at arm's length with the employer or who owns, directly or indirectly, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation—strict statutory limitations apply to prevent artificial remuneration shifting, capping claimable SR&ED salary and restricting proxy salary base inclusions.
Overhead Allocation: Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) vs. Traditional Method

On Line 160 of Form T661, every claimant must make an annual, irrevocable election for the taxation year to compute SR&ED overhead using either the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Method or the Traditional Method. Under Section 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations and Part 5 of Form T661, a taxpayer electing the PPA Method does not track or claim specific overhead expenditures within its SR&ED pool. Instead, the taxpayer computes a notional amount—the PPA—equal to 55% of the eligible SR&ED salary base of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada. While the PPA is not an actual cash outlay and therefore is not deducted under Section 37 (as the underlying office utilities, supplies, and support staff wages are already deducted as ordinary business expenses), the 55% PPA is included in total qualified SR&ED expenditures to earn both the federal ITC (35% or 15%) and applicable provincial R&D tax credits. Under the proxy method, claimants are explicitly prohibited from claiming lease costs for general-purpose office equipment or furniture (GPOEF) on Form T661.

Conversely, under the Traditional Method, the PPA is nil, and the taxpayer must itemise, substantiate, and allocate specific overhead and other expenditures on Line 360 of Form T661 that are directly related and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. While software, SaaS, and engineering firms almost universally elect the 55% Proxy Method because their direct labour-to-overhead ratio makes a 55% uplift far more lucrative and simpler to substantiate, heavy industrial manufacturers, mining firms, or utilities operating dedicated R&D pilot facilities with massive utility, shop-floor, and sub-90% equipment lease costs frequently model both methods and elect the Traditional Method when itemised incremental factory overheads exceed 55% of direct SR&ED wages.
Materials, Cloud Computing Infrastructure, and Subcontractors

Claimants may include the cost of physical materials that are either consumed (rendered virtually value-less or destroyed during experimental trials) or transformed (incorporated into an experimental prototype or pilot plant where the material ceases to exist in its original form) in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. In contemporary software, data analytics, and artificial intelligence SR&ED claims, cloud computing expenditures—such as Amazon Web Services (AWS), Google Cloud Platform (GCP), and Microsoft Azure GPU compute instances—represent a vital cost category. Under CRA administrative practice, elastic cloud computing resources used directly to execute experimental runs, train novel machine learning architectures, or benchmark algorithmic hypotheses are eligible as materials consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED (or as directly attributable traditional overhead where applicable), provided the claimant maintains granular telemetry or billing segregation separating experimental environments from commercial production hosting.

Where a claimant engages an arm's-length contractor to perform SR&ED in Canada on the claimant's behalf—under an SR&ED contract for basic research, applied research, experimental development, or eligible support work where the claimant retains the right to exploit the resulting intellectual property—80% of the eligible contract payment qualifies as a qualified SR&ED expenditure for ITC purposes. The statutory 20% reduction accounts for the contractor's assumed commercial profit margin and non-SR&ED overhead. Payments to foreign subcontractors performing work outside Canada are strictly ineligible for SR&ED, as all contract work must be performed within Canada. For non-arm's-length contractors, the 80% rule does not apply; instead, the performer's actual qualified SR&ED expenditures must be tracked and may be transferred to the commissioner using Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length), with related assistance allocated using Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length), and Line 540 of Form T661. Similarly, third-party payments in money or in kind made to approved universities, colleges, research institutes, or non-profit R&D corporations to carry out SR&ED in Canada related to the claimant's business qualify for SR&ED tax incentives provided the claimant is entitled to exploit the results.
Restoration of Capital Expenditures and Shared-Use Equipment (Post-December 15, 2024)

The enactment of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, restored the eligibility of SR&ED capital expenditures and capital lease costs for depreciable property acquired (and available for use) after December 15, 2024. Expenditures for depreciable property acquired before December 16, 2024, or lease costs incurred before December 16, 2024, remain strictly ineligible. As detailed in the CRA's updated Form T661 instructions released on May 15, 2026, capital property and equipment lease costs are governed by three rigorous statutory usage regimes.

First, under the All or Substantially All (ASA) regime, an expenditure to acquire new or used depreciable property after December 15, 2024, qualifies 100% as an SR&ED capital expenditure (reported on Lines 262, 263, and 535 of Form T661) if, at the time of acquisition, the claimant intended either to use the property all or substantially all (defined administratively as 90% or more) of its operating time over its expected useful life to perform SR&ED in Canada, or to consume 90% or more of its value in performing SR&ED in Canada. Land, which is a non-depreciable asset, and buildings are statutorily excluded from SR&ED capital expenditures even if used exclusively for R&D.

Second, for new depreciable equipment (excluding general-purpose office equipment or furniture) acquired after December 15, 2024, that does not meet the 90% ASA threshold, but is used primarily (more than 50% of its operating time) for SR&ED in Canada during its initial operating windows, Bill C-15 restored the first-term and second-term Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) regime on Line 504 of Form T661. If the equipment meets the requirements of both first-term and second-term SUE, a claimant may include 25% of the capital cost of the equipment in qualified SR&ED expenditures in the first period (first-term SUE) and an additional 25% of the capital cost in the second period (second-term SUE), bringing total qualified capital cost inclusion to 50%. Claimants must specifically list and identify on Form T661 the 20 most expensive SUE properties acquired after December 15, 2024.

Third, for leased equipment, lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, qualify if the equipment meets the capital eligibility rules (excluding GPOEF under the proxy method). Furthermore, if the claimant elects the Traditional Method on Line 160, lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, for equipment used in SR&ED less than 90% of the time may be claimed on Line 360 as overhead and other expenditures. For straddle taxation years that began before December 16, 2024, and ended after December 15, 2024, claimants must calculate the SR&ED operating time percentage strictly as a percentage of total operating time for the period after December 15, 2024, and may only include lease outlays incurred after December 15, 2024.
Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes and Inter-Jurisdictional Stacking
Provincial and Territorial R&D Incentives Matrix

In addition to the federal SR&ED program, Canadian provinces offer dedicated R&D tax credits or tax-system grants that stack with the federal credit. Except for Quebec (administered independently by Revenu Québec) and Alberta (administered through the Alberta corporate tax system), provincial R&D tax credits are administered jointly by the CRA through the federal T2 corporate tax return and piggyback directly on the federal definition of SR&ED in Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act.

body.text: Deep Dive: British Columbia's 2026 Harmonisation and Alberta's IEG Divergence

A comparative analysis of Western Canada's two largest innovation economies—British Columbia and Alberta—illustrates how provincial legislative design creates sharply divergent tax recovery profiles under the post-Bill C-15 regime. Historically, the British Columbia SR&ED tax credit under Part 6 (Section 97) of the Income Tax Act (B.C.) required periodic legislative extensions and was previously slated to sunset on September 1, 2027. In Budget 2026, through Bill 2 (Budget Measures Implementation Act, 2026), the Government of British Columbia made the 10% BC SR&ED tax credit permanent. Furthermore, British Columbia enacted full statutory harmonisation with the federal Bill C-15 reforms effective for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024.

Under British Columbia's harmonised framework, qualifying CCPCs and Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) with a permanent establishment in British Columbia can claim a 10% refundable BC SR&ED tax credit on the lesser of the corporation's SR&ED qualified BC expenditure for the taxation year and its federal expenditure limit, which is now $6,000,000. The prior-year taxable capital phase-out for the BC refundable limit expanded in lockstep with federal Subsection 127(10.2) to the $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 band, and capital expenditures acquired after December 15, 2024, were restored as BC qualified expenditures. Qualifying corporations that are not CCPCs or ECPCs, active corporate members of partnerships, and CCPCs or ECPCs with BC qualified expenditures exceeding the $6,000,000 expenditure limit may claim a 10% non-refundable BC SR&ED tax credit (reduced by any refundable credit claimed and any amount renounced under Subsection 100(1) of the British Columbia Income Tax Act). Consequently, a CCPC with full expenditure room that incurs $10,000,000 of eligible BC SR&ED expenditures generates $600,000 in refundable BC credits on the first $6,000,000 plus $400,000 in non-refundable BC credits on the remaining $4,000,000, whereas a foreign-controlled non-CCPC spending $10,000,000 generates $1,000,000 of non-refundable BC credits. Claimants must file Form T666 (British Columbia (BC) Scientific Research and Experimental Development Tax Credit) and report the refundable credit on Line 674 and the non-refundable credit on Line 659 of Schedule 5 (Tax Calculation Supplementary – Corporations) no later than 18 months after the end of the taxation year. Unused non-refundable BC credits may be carried back 3 taxation years and carried forward 10 taxation years. Additionally, BC video game, virtual reality, and interactive software studios can claim the BC Interactive Digital Media Tax Credit (IDMTC)—a 17.5% refundable tax credit on eligible BC labour expenses certified by Creative BC—which can complement SR&ED on distinct project activities to recover over 50% of a digital media development budget.

Unlike British Columbia, Alberta eliminated its former provincial SR&ED credit for the entirety of calendar year 2020 (causing Alberta claimants to lose between 12 and 23 months of provincial credits depending on their fiscal year-end) before introducing the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) for eligible R&D expenditures incurred in Alberta after December 31, 2020. Delivered through the corporate tax system without a separate pre-application process, the IEG provides a two-tier refundable tax credit on up to $4,000,000 in annual Alberta R&D spending that matches federal SR&ED eligibility criteria. Specifically, qualified corporations receive an 8% payment on eligible Alberta R&D spending up to the corporation's "base level of spending"—calculated as the corporation's average qualifying Alberta R&D spending over the previous two taxation years—and an enhanced 20% payment on incremental eligible R&D spending that exceeds that two-year average base level. Crucially, Alberta's IEG continues to phase out incrementally for corporations with prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000 under the legacy Subsection 127(10.2) thresholds, completely disqualifying firms with $50,000,000 or more in taxable capital even though they remain eligible for the federal 35% enhanced SR&ED credit up to $75,000,000 in taxable capital under Bill C-15.
Mathematical Mechanics of Federal-Provincial Stacking and the Government Assistance Grind

Under Subsection 127(9) of the federal Income Tax Act, provincial and territorial R&D tax credits (as well as direct government grants such as NRC IRAP) are statutorily defined as "government assistance". Government assistance earned in a taxation year reduces the federal pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures and qualified SR&ED expenditures before the federal SR&ED ITC is computed.

Let E represent a CCPC's total qualified SR&ED expenditures (including the 55% PPA on direct SR&ED salaries) within the $6,000,000 expenditure limit, let p represent the provincial R&D tax credit rate, and let f represent the enhanced federal SR&ED ITC rate. In jurisdictions where the provincial credit is calculated on the unreduced expenditure pool, the combined net effective tax credit rate on qualified expenditures (R) is governed by the sequential assistance grind equation: R = p + f × (1 − p)

Furthermore, when evaluating the net cash recovery on direct in-house SR&ED salaries (S) for a CCPC electing the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA), both the provincial credit (outside Quebec) and the federal 35% ITC apply to 1.55 × S. Consequently, in British Columbia, where the 10% refundable BC SR&ED credit and the 35% refundable federal SR&ED credit interact across Form T666 and Form T661, the blended effective recovery rate on total qualified expenditures sits in the high-30s to 45% before/after reciprocal assistance grinds, allowing startups and scaling CCPCs to recover up to 64% of direct SR&ED salary expenditures in non-dilutive cash.
Substantive Technical Eligibility: Jurisprudence and the CRA "Why" and "How" Framework
Statutory Definition of SR&ED: Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act

The legal threshold for whether a technical project qualifies for SR&ED tax incentives is codified in Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, which conforms generally to the OECD Frascati Manual and defines "scientific research and experimental development" as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis". The statute subdivides eligible investigations into three primary categories: basic research, defined in paragraph (a) as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view; applied research, defined in paragraph (b) as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view; and experimental development, defined in paragraph (c) as work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Paragraph (d) then incorporates support work with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research where such work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of basic research, applied research, or experimental development undertaken in Canada.

Subsection 248(1) also enforces explicit statutory exclusions, disqualifying market research or sales promotion, routine quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes, research in the social sciences or the humanities, routine data collection, and cosmetic or style changes to existing products.
Landmark Canadian Jurisprudence Governing SR&ED Audits and Appeals

Because the statutory phrasing in Subsection 248(1) is concise, the substantive meaning of "technological uncertainty," "systematic investigation," "technological advancement," and "routine engineering" has been forged through nearly three decades of Tax Court of Canada (TCC) and Federal Court of Appeal (FCA) jurisprudence.

cells: Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, 98 D.T.C. 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520

Judge (later Chief Justice) Donald Bowman established the canonical five-question test for determining SR&ED eligibility under s. 248(1), defining technological uncertainty in contrast to routine engineering.
Held that work must be performed for the purpose of achieving technological advancement and emphasized objective verification and documentation of experimental testing.
C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393
Formally adopted the five Northwest Hydraulic questions as appellate law across Canada (at para. 17) to evaluate whether a creative venture constitutes SR&ED.
Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen, 2014 TCC 313

Justice Jorré ruled (at para. 94) that while contemporaneous documentation may be necessary to resolve factual disputes, "the existence of contemporaneous documentation, or contemporaneous documents with specific intent, is not a condition to the recognition of scientific research or experimental development".
Hypercube Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 65, 2015 D.T.C. 1089
Denied an SR&ED claim involving a web "crawler" software program (at para. 48), holding that vague descriptions of employee tasks and routine software development fail the statutory test.
Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6

Justice Sommerfeldt (at para. 17) examined the concept of "routine engineering" and summarized the objective characteristics that must be present to demonstrate that the scientific method was adopted.
Clevor Technologies Inc. v. The Queen, 2019 TCC 166
Justice Russell (at para. 11) reaffirmed the rigorous application of the five-question Northwest Hydraulic and C.W. Agencies framework.
Dock Edge + Inc. v. The Queen, 2019 TCC (2016-539)
Clarified that "technological advancement" means an advancement in general understanding rather than merely company-specific knowledge within a single business.
National R & D Inc. v. The Queen, 2020 TCC 47

Justice Lafleur (at para. 67) confirmed that there is no statutory requirement that all SR&ED evidence be documentary; credible oral testimonial evidence supported by contemporaneous coding notes is acceptable.
Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King, TCC (2025)

Found in favour of the taxpayer on a food-science shelf-stability claim (exploding cans of cold-pressed juice caused by microbial oxygen release without heat pasteurisation), holding that the taxpayer proved on a balance of probabilities that the uncertainty could not be resolved by routine engineering and was addressed via the scientific method.

body.text: The Five Questions of Northwest Hydraulic and the CRA's Consolidated "Why" and "How" Guidelines

The bedrock of Canadian SR&ED audit practice is the five-question test articulated by Judge Bowman in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen (1998) and affirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen (2001) at paragraph 17. First, was there a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures? Second, did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty? Third, did the procedure adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of the hypotheses? Fourth, did the process result in a technological advancement? Fifth, was a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and the results kept as the work progressed?

As explained in the CRA's A Brief History of Guidance on the Eligibility of Work, the CRA's consolidated eligibility guidelines distill the five Northwest Hydraulic questions and the statutory definition in Subsection 248(1) into two foundational requirements—the "Why" requirement and the "How" requirement—to provide a common language for claimants and CRA officials. The "Why" requirement addresses the scientific or technological advancement sought (encompassing Questions 1 and 4): work must be conducted to generate information that advances the understanding of scientific relations or technologies by overcoming a scientific or technological uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures. As demonstrated in Dock Edge + Inc. v. The Queen (2019), this technological advancement must represent an advancement in general scientific or technological understanding rather than simply acquiring knowledge that was new only to the claimant company.

The "How" requirement addresses the systematic investigation or search (encompassing Questions 2, 3, and 5): the claimant must follow the objective principles of the scientific method by formulating hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating the technological uncertainty, testing and modifying those hypotheses through experiment or analysis, and maintaining records as the work progresses. Notably, in Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen (2014 TCC 313, at para. 94) and National R & D Inc. v. The Queen (2020 TCC 47, at para. 67), the Tax Court of Canada emphasized that while failing to keep contemporaneous documentation creates severe evidentiary risks during a factual dispute with the Minister, the existence of contemporaneous documentary records is not a strict statutory pre-condition to the recognition of SR&ED, and credible witness testimony supported by coding notes or test logs can satisfy the burden of proof on a balance of probabilities. This principle was recently reinforced in Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King (2025), where the Tax Court accepted the taxpayer's testimony and testing records showing how her food scientists systematically formulated and tested preservative hypotheses to prevent microbial oxygen release from exploding cans of unpasteurised cold-pressed juice.
Administrative Filing Procedures, Prescribed Forms, and Audit Defence
Mandatory Tax Forms and the May 2026 Post-Bill C-15 Revisions

Following Royal Assent of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, the Canada Revenue Agency issued updated versions of all primary SR&ED prescribed forms in May 2026 to accommodate the $6,000,000 expenditure limit, the $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 taxable capital phase-out, ECPC eligibility, the CCPC revenue election, and the restoration of capital expenditures and Shared-Use Equipment. Specifically, the CRA updated Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim) and Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) on May 15, 2026, followed by Schedule T2SCH31 (Schedule 31, Investment Tax Credit – Corporations) on May 22, 2026, and Schedule T2SCH49 (Schedule 49, Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit) on May 29, 2026.

body.text: Statutory Filing Deadlines and CRA Service Standards

Under the Income Tax Act, a taxpayer's SR&ED reporting deadline is strictly 12 months after the filing due date of the taxpayer's income tax return for the taxation year in which the expenditures were incurred. Because a corporation's T2 income tax return is due 6 months after the end of its taxation year, the corporate SR&ED filing deadline for Form T661 and Schedule 31 is exactly 18 months after the end of its taxation year. For example, a corporation with a December 31, 2024 taxation year-end faces an absolute filing deadline of June 30, 2026; a corporation with a December 31, 2025 taxation year-end must file Form T661 by June 30, 2027; and a corporation with a March 31, 2026 taxation year-end must file by September 30, 2027. For individuals carrying on an unincorporated business, the SR&ED filing deadline is 17.5 months after the end of the calendar taxation year (mid-June of the second following year, such as mid-June 2027 for the 2025 calendar year).

The CRA does not grant administrative extensions to the 18-month filing deadline except in narrow statutory circumstances, making timely filing essential to preserve entitlement to both federal and provincial credits. Tax practitioners strongly recommend filing well ahead of the 18-month mark—ideally with the original T2 return—to leave adequate room for CRA clarification requests. For complete claims that are not selected for a technical or financial review, the CRA's target processing standard is 60 days.
Complementary Innovation Grants, IP Incentives, and Clean Economy Stacking
Strategic Stacking: NRC IRAP and Direct Government Grants

Canada's tax credit regime operates alongside a substantial suite of direct federal innovation funding programs that can be strategically stacked with SR&ED. The premier direct grant program for small and medium-sized businesses is the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP), which provides non-dilutive financial support to Canadian SMBs undertaking technology innovation projects. Because an NRC IRAP contribution constitutes government assistance, it reduces the federal and provincial SR&ED qualified expenditure pools. However, because the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) on Part 5 of Form T661 is computed on the gross eligible SR&ED salary base prior to deducting government assistance, stacking NRC IRAP with SR&ED yields a highly favourable combined recovery rate when properly coordinated.

Beyond NRC IRAP, Federal Budget 2024 (Fairness for Every Generation) introduced extensive complementary research and innovation investments across the Canadian ecosystem. Specifically, Budget 2024 allocated $1.8 billion over five years, starting in 2024–25 (with $748.3 million per year ongoing), to increase core research grant funding for the three federal granting councils—the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council (NSERC), the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council (SSHRC), and the Canadian Institutes of Health Research (CIHR)—alongside $26.9 million over five years to establish a new Capstone Research Funding Organization and an additional $26.9 million over five years to modernise and harmonise federal grant management systems. Furthermore, Budget 2024 committed $158.5 million over two years to the Regional Economic Growth through Innovation (REGI) program (building on $200 million dedicated to AI adoption), $60 million over five years to Futurpreneur Canada to empower young entrepreneurs, and $3.1 billion over 11 years starting in 2025–26 to Atomic Energy of Canada Limited to support Canadian Nuclear Laboratories' nuclear science research.
Intellectual Property Retention, Patent Box Consultations, and Immediate Expensing

To encourage the development and retention of intellectual property within Canada and ensure that innovative Canadian businesses remain domestically owned and operated, the federal government paired its 2024–2026 SR&ED reforms with targeted IP and capital investment incentives. In Budget 2024, the government proposed the creation of a federal patent box regime and conducted formal consultations on taxing income earned from Canadian-developed intellectual property at a preferential corporate tax rate. Simultaneously, Budget 2024 provided $14.5 million over two years, starting in 2024–25, to Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED) for the Innovation Asset Collective to assist small and medium-sized businesses in leveraging and defending their intellectual property rights.

In parallel with the restoration of SR&ED capital expenditures under Bill C-15, the federal government enacted a temporary 100% immediate expensing measure allowing businesses to immediately write off the full cost of new investments in patents, data network infrastructure equipment, computers, and other data processing equipment put into use before January 1, 2027. Furthermore, within the broader clean technology ecosystem, Budget 2024 delivered key components of the federal government's $160 billion clean growth framework—including the Clean Electricity Investment Tax Credit, the Clean Fuels Fund extension ($776.3 million), and amendments to the Clean Technology Manufacturing Investment Tax Credit to clarify access for polymetallic critical minerals projects—providing capital-intensive innovators with multiple non-dilutive tax credit pathways depending on whether capital assets are deployed in experimental R&D or commercial clean-tech manufacturing.
Strategic Conclusions and Audit Risk Mitigation Recommendations

The enactment of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, fundamentally alters tax planning and R&D capital allocation in Canada for all taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. First, growing CCPCs with prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada between $10,000,000 and $75,000,000 must immediately update their Schedule 49 expenditure limit models to reflect the doubled $6,000,000 limit and the expanded $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 phase-out band, while capital-intensive CCPCs with high balance-sheet capital should evaluate the Subsection 127(10.31) election to use the three-year average gross revenue phase-out formula. Second, public corporations resident in Canada and listed on designated stock exchanges must evaluate their eligibility as Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) under Subsection 127(9) and compute their three-year consolidated gross revenue under Subsection 127(10.62) to access the 35% federal and 10% British Columbia refundable credits.

Third, because Bill C-15 restored SR&ED capital expenditures (90% ASA test) and Shared-Use Equipment (50%+ first-term and second-term SUE on Line 504) for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, hardware, biotechnology, clean-tech, and AI companies acquiring GPU clusters or laboratory apparatus must institute contemporaneous operating-time logs to substantiate the percentage of total operating time devoted to SR&ED after December 15, 2024. Fourth, software and AI claimants utilizing AWS, GCP, or Azure cloud computing environments must segregate experimental training runs from commercial hosting so that cloud compute costs are defensibly documented as materials consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED. Finally, technical leads drafting Form T661 narratives on Lines 242, 244, and 246 must avoid describing commercial product features or routine software debugging as seen in Hypercube Inc. v. The Queen (2015 TCC 65), and instead document why the technological uncertainty could not be resolved through routine engineering, how hypotheses were systematically formulated and tested under the scientific method as validated in Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King (2025), and what general technological advancements were achieved.
